question: On Gram staining of tissue from a suspected gas gangrene wound, which finding is MOST pathognomonic of Clostridium perfringens myonecrosis?

answers.text: Large Gram-positive rods in the ABSENCE of polymorphonuclear leucocytes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Alpha toxin (lecithinase/phospholipase C) destroys leucocytes as fast as they arrive, producing the pathognomonic finding of Gram-positive rods WITHOUT PMNs. Pus with gas suggests mixed infection (type I necrotising fasciitis), not pure clostridial myonecrosis.

answers.text: Gram-positive rods surrounded by abundant PMNs and pus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Abundant PMNs with gas points to a mixed (type I) necrotising fasciitis, not pure clostridial gas gangrene. Alpha toxin kills PMNs, so their ABSENCE is the diagnostic clue.

answers.text: Gram-negative rods with gas bubbles visible on the smear

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. C. perfringens is a Gram-POSITIVE rod, not Gram-negative. Gas is detected clinically by crepitus on palpation or on X-ray, not directly on Gram stain.

answers.text: Gram-positive cocci in clusters with surrounding leucocytosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Gram-positive cocci in clusters describes Staphylococcus aureus, not Clostridia. C. perfringens appears as large Gram-positive rods with a characteristic box-car morphology.

overallFeedback.feedback: The pathognomonic finding is large Gram-positive rods WITHOUT PMNs — alpha toxin kills leucocytes faster than they arrive. PMNs + gas = mixed infection, not pure clostridial gangrene.
Well done! The absence of PMNs is the key — alpha toxin (phospholipase C) lyses leucocytes, making this the opposite of typical pyogenic infections where PMNs are abundant.
